name: Pallas
production_evidence: Used in production for TPU-based inference at Google
Part of the JAX ecosystem, which is used for production TPU serving
strengths: TPU-native: the only Python DSL that targets TPUs with good performance
JAX integration: seamless with JAX transformations (jit, vmap, grad)
Pipelining: emit_pipeline handles double-buffering and memory/compute overlap automatically
Memory space abstraction: explicit HBM/VMEM management matches TPU architecture
SparseCore support: can target TPU SparseCores for structured sparsity
weaknesses: TPU-only: no NVIDIA or AMD GPU support
No autotuning: block sizes and other parameters must be chosen manually
Smaller community than Triton: fewer examples, less documentation
JAX dependency: requires JAX, which is a heavy dependency for kernel-only use
Less mature than Triton: newer project, fewer production deployments
notes: Pallas is a Python DSL for writing TPU kernels, analogous to Triton for GPUs. It is part of the JAX ecosystem and provides a higher-level abstraction than raw XLA. The key concept is the Ref (mutable array reference) which lives in a specific memory space (HBM or VMEM). Kernels operate on VMEM Refs, and data must be explicitly copied between HBM and VMEM. The emit_pipeline function handles pipelining (overlapping memory transfers with compute) automatically. The matmul tutorial shows real TPU performance: 91% FLOP/s utilization at 8192x8192x8192 with bf16, which is competitive with hand-optimized TPU kernels. Pallas is the recommended way to write custom TPU kernels, just as Triton is for NVIDIA GPUs. The main limitation is TPU-only support: there is no path to NVIDIA or AMD GPUs. For teams standardizing on TPUs, Pallas is the clear choice. For GPU-based inference, Triton is the alternative.
